description: I'm a software engineer from Bulgaria working in the games industry, with experience in C#, Unity, real-time systems and AI tools. I've always been fascinated by astronomy and the night sky, so the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge felt like the perfect fit. I'm participating solo this time - looking forward to exploring real SPHEREx data and building something useful and accessible during the hackathon!
summary:
PlutoX 0723+21 is a public web tool that blinks real SPHEREx images of any patch of sky, epoch by epoch - the way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930. Users start in a live 3D sky of Gaia DR3 stars, pick one of the five challenge targets or enter any RA/Dec, and watch per-epoch SPHEREx frames play like a short video, with Difference and Stack modes, a predicted-position track, a six-detector wavelength rail and spectra on the fly. Every frame shows its date, detector, wavelength and data release, and saturation is flagged rather than hidden. On the test objects it reproduces Barnard's Star's northward motion (≈10.4″ in about a year), consistent with Gaia DR3.
SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands - far more data than any one person can inspect. By making its images easy to compare over time and wavelength, PlutoX lets students, volunteers and scientists alike look for moving and changing objects, such as nearby brown dwarfs, and check every result against its source data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

PlutoX 0723+21 turns SPHEREx images into a time machine for any patch of sky. For a target or any RA/Dec, it searches the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive for SPHEREx Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3 spectral images, reads only the needed rows of each file from IRSA's public AWS mirror, removes zodiacal light, resamples every exposure to one north-up 6.15″ grid and combines them into an inverse-variance stack per survey epoch and detector. Positions are propagated with Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 proper motions, so fast movers such as WISE 0855-0714 (now about 2′ from its 2010 coordinates) stay centred. Three views connect the scales: Sky (a live 3D sky of about 107,000 Gaia DR3 stars), Time machine (blinking frames with Difference and Stack modes, a predicted-position track and a D1-D6 wavelength rail) and Pixel scale (a spectrum from all six detectors, light curves and a time × wavelength matrix). A deterministic guide answers questions only from the loaded measurements, with citations and confidence levels.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SPHEREx produces far more data than anyone can inspect by hand. PlutoX makes it easy for students, volunteers and scientists to see what moves or changes, in the spirit of citizen-science projects such as Backyard Worlds, while keeping every result traceable to its file, epoch, detector and wavelength.

CREATIVITY

The project reimagines Tombaugh's 1930 blink comparison - its name is Pluto's position on the discovery plate, 07h23m +21°50′ - and adds SPHEREx's spectral dimension: users travel through time and wavelength together, and can watch a cold brown dwarf appear only at the longest wavelengths.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty first: frames are compared only within a detector because SPHEREx's wavelength changes across each image; saturation is flagged, never hidden; nothing is called a discovery. We validated the method on the test objects (Barnard's Star moves ≈10.4″ north in about a year, consistent with Gaia DR3 to about 0.5-1″). The archive was often unavailable during the hackathon, so the five targets are precomputed from real data and one command regenerates them for new releases. Accessibility, mobile use and full credits were part of the design.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy), TypeScript with Vite and WebGL, Docker, Render; data from NASA SPHEREx, ESA Gaia, AllWISE/CatWISE2020 and Hipparcos.
